items.followUp: State two differences between the electronic arrangement in Rutherford’s model and Bohr’s model of the atom.

rubric.why: A key difference is whether electrons occupy fixed energy levels.
rubric.description: Rutherford’s model has no fixed energy levels; Bohr’s model has definite energy levels.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly contrasting the absence of fixed energy levels in Rutherford’s model with Bohr’s definite energy levels.

rubric.why: Bohr’s stationary orbits explain atomic stability, unlike Rutherford’s model.
rubric.description: Rutherford’s model could not explain atomic stability; Bohr’s stationary orbits explain why electrons do not radiate energy while in them.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct contrast about stability or energy radiation in the two models.

modelAnswer: In Rutherford’s model, electrons can revolve around the nucleus at any distance; in Bohr’s model, they revolve in fixed orbits with definite energy levels.
Rutherford’s model could not explain the stability of the atom; Bohr proposed that electrons in stationary orbits do not radiate energy.

items.followUp: Name the elements present in the second period of the periodic table.

rubric.why: Hydrogen is one of the two elements in the first period.
Helium is the other element in the first period.

modelAnswer: The elements of the first period are hydrogen (H) and helium (He).

items.followUp: Why are the elements of the f-block shown in two rows below the main body of the periodic table?

rubric.why: Separating these series prevents the periodic table from becoming too wide.
rubric.description: States that the separate placement saves space or keeps the table compact.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid explanation based on the table’s size or layout.

rubric.why: These series belong to the sixth and seventh periods, respectively.
rubric.description: Identifies the lanthanides and actinides as the two series associated with periods 6 and 7.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly connecting the series to the sixth and seventh periods.

modelAnswer: Lanthanides and actinides are placed separately below the periodic table to keep it compact and avoid making it too wide.
The lanthanides belong to the sixth period and the actinides to the seventh period.

items.followUp: Define a suspension and give one example.

accept: homogeneous mixture of solute and solvent
rubric.why: A solution is a homogeneous mixture of its components.
rubric.description: Defines a solution as a homogeneous mixture of solute and solvent.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct definition.

rubric.why: A suitable example demonstrates the meaning of a solution.
rubric.description: Gives a valid example of a solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct example.

modelAnswer: A solution is a homogeneous mixture of a solute and a solvent.
Salt dissolved in water is an example of a solution.

items.followUp: What is a non-polar compound? Give one example.

rubric.why: Unequal sharing of electrons in a covalent bond creates polarity.
rubric.description: States that electrons are shared unequally, commonly because one atom attracts them more strongly.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying unequal sharing of electrons or the cause of unequal sharing.

rubric.why: Unequal electron distribution produces separated partial charges and a dipole.
rubric.description: States that the compound has separated charges or a positive and a negative pole.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the resulting charge separation or dipole.

modelAnswer: A polar compound is a covalent compound in which the shared electrons are attracted more strongly by one atom, so they are shared unequally.
This unequal sharing creates partial positive and negative ends, producing a dipole.

items.followUp: Name the types of chemical bonds and give one example of each.

rubric.why: The ionic bond is one of the principal types of chemical bond.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming an ionic bond.

rubric.why: Covalent bonding, including coordinate covalent bonding, is another type of chemical bond.
rubric.description: Names a covalent bond or a coordinate covalent bond.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming a covalent or coordinate covalent bond.

modelAnswer: The types of chemical bonds are ionic bonds, covalent bonds and coordinate covalent bonds.

items.followUp: Define boiling and state how it differs from evaporation.

rubric.why: Evaporation occurs at the surface of a liquid.
rubric.description: Identifies the surface as the place where evaporation occurs.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that evaporation occurs at the liquid’s surface.

rubric.why: Evaporation is the change of liquid into vapour and can occur below the boiling point.
rubric.description: States that liquid changes into vapour, at any temperature or below its boiling point.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the change into vapour or its temperature condition.

modelAnswer: Evaporation is the change of a liquid into vapour from its surface.
It can occur at any temperature below the boiling point of the liquid.

items.followUp: How does increasing the temperature affect the vapour pressure of a liquid?

rubric.why: The nature of a liquid’s intermolecular attractions influences how easily its molecules escape.
rubric.description: Connects vapour pressure with the strength of intermolecular forces or molecular attraction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying intermolecular attraction as the relevant property of the liquid.

rubric.why: Weaker attractions allow more molecules to escape, increasing vapour pressure; stronger attractions reduce it.
rubric.description: Correctly relates weaker attractions to higher vapour pressure or stronger attractions to lower vapour pressure.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct relationship between the nature of the liquid and its vapour pressure.

modelAnswer: Vapour pressure depends on the strength of the intermolecular forces in the liquid.
Liquids with weaker intermolecular forces are more volatile and have higher vapour pressure; stronger forces give lower vapour pressure.
